# unit_prefix - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/unit-prefix/

## Expand description

This is a library for formatting numbers with numeric prefixes, such as turning “3000 metres” into “3 kilometres”, or “8705 bytes” into “8.5 KiB”.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The function [ NumberPrefix::decimal](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html#method.decimal)
returns either a pair of the resulting number and its prefix, or a
notice that the number was too small to have any prefix applied to it. For
example:

```
use unit_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    },
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
    },
};
assert_eq!("The file is 8.5 kB in size", result);
```
The `{:.1}` part of the formatting string tells it to restrict the
output to only one decimal place. This value is calculated by repeatedly
dividing the number by 1000 until it becomes less than that, which in this
case results in 8.542, which gets rounded down. Because only one division
had to take place, the function also returns the decimal prefix `Kilo`,
which gets converted to its internationally-recognised symbol when
formatted as a string.

If the value is too small to have any prefixes applied to it — in this case, if it’s under 1000 — then the standalone value will be returned:

```
use unit_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 705_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    },
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
    },
};
assert_eq!("The file is 705 bytes in size", result);
```
In this particular example, the user expects different formatting for both bytes and kilobytes: while prefixed values are given more precision, there’s no point using anything other than whole numbers for just byte amounts. This is why the function pays attention to values without any prefixes — they often need to be special-cased.

[§](https://docs.rs#binary-prefixes)Binary Prefixes

This library also allows you to use the *binary prefixes*, which use the
number 1024 (210) as the multiplier, rather than the more common 1000
(103). This uses the
[ NumberPrefix::binary](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html#method.binary) function.
For example:

```
use unit_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::binary(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    },
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
    },
};
assert_eq!("The file is 8.3 KiB in size", result);
```
A kibibyte is slightly larger than a kilobyte, so the number is smaller in the result; but other than that, it works in exactly the same way, with the binary prefix being converted to a symbol automatically.

[§](https://docs.rs#which-type-of-prefix-should-i-use)Which type of prefix should I use?

There is no correct answer this question! Common practice is to use
the binary prefixes for numbers of *bytes*, while still using the decimal
prefixes for everything else. Computers work with powers of two, rather than
powers of ten, and by using the binary prefixes, you get a more accurate
representation of the amount of data.

[§](https://docs.rs#prefix-names)Prefix Names

If you need to describe your unit in actual words, rather than just with the
symbol, use one of the `upper`, `caps`, `lower`, or `symbol`, which output the
prefix in a variety of formats. For example:

```
use unit_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    },
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}bytes in size", n, prefix.lower())
    },
};
assert_eq!("The file is 8.5 kilobytes in size", result);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#string-parsing)String Parsing

There is a `FromStr` implementation for `NumberPrefix` that parses
strings containing numbers and trailing prefixes, such as `7.5E`.

Currently, the only supported units are `b` and `B` for bytes, and `m` for
metres. Whitespace is allowed between the number and the rest of the string.

```
use unit_prefix::{NumberPrefix, Prefix};
assert_eq!(
    "7.05E".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
    Ok(NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Exa, 7.05_f64))
);
assert_eq!(
    "7.05".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
    Ok(NumberPrefix::Standalone(7.05_f64))
);
assert_eq!(
    "7.05 GiB".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
    Ok(NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Gibi, 7.05_f64))
);
```
## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Number](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html)- Prefix
- The result of trying to apply a prefix to a floating-point value.
- [Prefix](https://docs.rs/enum.Prefix.html)
- A numeric prefix, either binary or decimal.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Amounts](https://docs.rs/trait.Amounts.html)
- Traits for floating-point values for both the possible multipliers. They need to be Copy, have defined 1000 and 1024s, and implement a bunch of operators.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# http_request_zabbix - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/http-request-zabbix/0.2.1/http_request_zabbix/

## Expand description

A Rust library for interacting with the Zabbix API.

This crate provides a convenient and idiomatic way to communicate with a Zabbix server, handling authentication, version checking, and raw API requests.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use http_request_zabbix::{ZabbixInstance, AuthType};
let zabbix = ZabbixInstance::builder("http://zabbix.example.com/zabbix")
    .build()
    .unwrap()
    .login(AuthType::UsernamePassword("Admin".to_string(), "zabbix".to_string()))
    .unwrap();
println!("Zabbix Version: {}", zabbix.get_version().unwrap());
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Zabbix](https://docs.rs/struct.ZabbixInstance.html)- Instance
- Represents an active connection to a Zabbix server.
- [Zabbix](https://docs.rs/struct.ZabbixInstanceBuilder.html)- Instance - Builder
- A builder for creating a `ZabbixInstance`.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [ApiRequest](https://docs.rs/enum.ApiRequestParams.html)- Params
- An enum representing the types of parameters that can be passed to the Zabbix API.
- [Auth](https://docs.rs/enum.AuthType.html)- Type
- Enum representing the type of authentication to use.
- [Zabbix](https://docs.rs/enum.ZabbixError.html)- Error
- Error type for Zabbix interactions.

# micpipe 0.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/micpipe/0.1.0

# micpipe

`micpipe` is a lightweight macOS audio router service for sending your
microphone into `BlackHole 2ch` or another CoreAudio output. It is built for the
common workflow of using BlackHole as the microphone source in another app while
keeping the route alive in the background.

It can also run in the foreground while you are testing.

## What it does

- Routes one input device to one output device.
- Runs as a per-user `launchd`service.
- Follows the system default input, or pins a specific input by name.
- Restarts automatically when the default input disconnects.
- Waits for a pinned input to reconnect, then restarts automatically.

## What it is not

`micpipe` is not a full multi-source mixer. It does not currently combine
multiple inputs, expose gain controls, or provide mute/solo controls. It is a
small background audio router for keeping a microphone-to-output route alive.

## Requirements

- macOS
- Rust and Cargo
- BlackHole, or another CoreAudio output device to receive the microphone audio
- Microphone permission for the terminal or installed binary that runs `micpipe`

## Install

Install from crates.io:

```
```
Install from a source checkout:

```
```
## Quick start

Run in the foreground with the default route:

```
```
By default, `micpipe run` follows the system default input device and routes it
to the first output device whose description contains `BlackHole 2ch`.

Install and start the background service:

```
```
Pin explicit devices when you want stable matching by device-name substring:

```
```
Use `run` instead of `install` for foreground testing:

```
```
Add `--debug` to log buffer occupancy once per second:

```
```
## Common use cases

- Send your mic into BlackHole so another app can select BlackHole as its input.
- Keep that route alive as a background service.
- Follow whichever microphone is currently the macOS default.
- Pin a USB or external microphone and restart only after that same device reconnects.

## macOS setup notes

Install BlackHole separately before using the default output route.

Run `micpipe run` once from the terminal if macOS needs to prompt for microphone
permission. The permission belongs to the app or binary that starts `micpipe`, so
the foreground test is the easiest way to confirm capture works before installing
the service.

## CLI reference

```
micpipe run [--input <name>] [--output <name>] [--debug]
micpipe install [--input <name>] [--output <name>] [--debug]
micpipe status
micpipe restart
micpipe stop
micpipe start
micpipe uninstall
```
`--output` is a case-insensitive substring match and defaults to
`BlackHole 2ch`.

`--input` is optional:

- Without `--input`,`micpipe`follows the system default input device. If that input disconnects,`micpipe`logs that the input device was disconnected and immediately asks the installed service to restart.
- With `--input`,`micpipe`pins that input by case-insensitive substring. If the pinned input disconnects,`micpipe`logs the disconnected device, polls every 5 seconds until that input appears again, then asks the installed service to restart.

Output stream errors are logged, but do not currently trigger a restart.

## Service

`micpipe install` records the current executable path in the plist. When you
install from crates.io, that is usually the `micpipe` binary under Cargo's bin
directory.

Useful service commands:

```
```
The service label is `com.markarranz.micpipe`, and the generated plist lives at:

```
~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.markarranz.micpipe.plist
```
Re-run `micpipe uninstall` followed by `micpipe install ...` when you want to
change the installed route arguments.

## Logs

The service writes logs under:

```
~/.local/share/micpipe/out.log
~/.local/share/micpipe/err.log
```
Watch both logs with:

```
```
Log lines are timestamped in the user's local timezone with a numeric offset, for example:

```
[2026-06-29T13:04:05-07:00] Mic -> BlackHole running...
```
Human-facing lifecycle and recovery messages go to `out.log`. Raw stream errors
and restart-command failures go to `err.log`.

When the default input disconnects, `out.log` includes a recovery message like:

```
[2026-06-29T13:04:05-07:00] input device disconnected: MacBook Pro Microphone; attempting micpipe restart
```
When a pinned input disconnects, `out.log` records that `micpipe` is waiting for
that device before restarting:

```
[2026-06-29T13:04:05-07:00] input device disconnected: USB Microphone; waiting for pinned input device 'USB Microphone' to reconnect before restarting
[2026-06-29T13:04:10-07:00] pinned input device reconnected: USB Microphone; attempting micpipe restart
```
## Troubleshooting

### No output device matching BlackHole

Install BlackHole, confirm it appears in macOS audio devices, or pass a different output substring:

```
```
### No default input device

Select a default microphone in macOS Sound settings, or pass an explicit input:

```
```
### Service installed but not loaded

Start it again and then inspect status:

```
```
### Logs show input device disconnected

If you are following the default input, `micpipe` attempts an immediate service
restart. If you pinned an input with `--input`, reconnect that same device;
`micpipe` polls every 5 seconds and restarts after it appears again.

### Route arguments changed

Uninstall and reinstall the service so the plist is regenerated with the new arguments:

```
```
## Development

Run the checks before committing changes:

```
```
After changing the binary for an installed service:

```
```
See [DESIGN.md](https://docs.rs/DESIGN.md) for implementation details.

# ru 0.1.14 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ru/0.1.14

## ru

ru is a simple and easy-to-use cli tool inspired by `du` to find out the disk usage of files/directories.

The motivation behind this project is to have a safe, performant and cross platform way to measure disk usage of folders and files.

### Usage

Install the tool:

```
cargo install ru
```
Use the tool with the `ru` binary:

```
ru .
```
### Contributing

Issues are welcome, if you find a bug and want to report it I will be pleased to fix it if i have the time for it.

PRs are not welcome, only the changes I want or need will be implemented, if you feel that this is not "right", fork it.

# glutton_westend_runtime - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/glutton-westend-runtime/28.0.0/glutton_westend_runtime/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#glutton-westend-runtime)Glutton Westend Runtime

The purpose of the Glutton parachain is to do stress testing on the Kusama network. This runtime targets the Westend runtime to allow development separate to the Kusama runtime.

There may be multiple instances of the Glutton parachain deployed and connected to its parent relay chain.

These parachains are not holding any real value. Their purpose is to stress test the network.

[§](https://docs.rs#governance)Governance

Glutton defers its governance (namely, its `Root` origin), to its Relay
Chain parent, Kusama (or Westend for development purposes).

[§](https://docs.rs#xcm)XCM

Since the main goal of Glutton is solely stress testing, the parachain will only be able receive XCM messages from the Relay Chain via DMP. This way the Glutton parachains will be able to listen for upgrades that are coming from the Relay chain.

# unit_prefix - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/unit-prefix/0.5.2/target-redirect/unit_prefix/

## Expand description

This is a library for formatting numbers with numeric prefixes, such as turning “3000 metres” into “3 kilometres”, or “8705 bytes” into “8.5 KiB”.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The function [ NumberPrefix::decimal](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html#method.decimal)
returns either a pair of the resulting number and its prefix, or a
notice that the number was too small to have any prefix applied to it. For
example:

```
use unit_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    },
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
    },
};
assert_eq!("The file is 8.5 kB in size", result);
```
The `{:.1}` part of the formatting string tells it to restrict the
output to only one decimal place. This value is calculated by repeatedly
dividing the number by 1000 until it becomes less than that, which in this
case results in 8.542, which gets rounded down. Because only one division
had to take place, the function also returns the decimal prefix `Kilo`,
which gets converted to its internationally-recognised symbol when
formatted as a string.

If the value is too small to have any prefixes applied to it — in this case, if it’s under 1000 — then the standalone value will be returned:

```
use unit_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 705_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    },
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
    },
};
assert_eq!("The file is 705 bytes in size", result);
```
In this particular example, the user expects different formatting for both bytes and kilobytes: while prefixed values are given more precision, there’s no point using anything other than whole numbers for just byte amounts. This is why the function pays attention to values without any prefixes — they often need to be special-cased.

[§](https://docs.rs#binary-prefixes)Binary Prefixes

This library also allows you to use the *binary prefixes*, which use the
number 1024 (210) as the multiplier, rather than the more common 1000
(103). This uses the
[ NumberPrefix::binary](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html#method.binary) function.
For example:

```
use unit_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::binary(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    },
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
    },
};
assert_eq!("The file is 8.3 KiB in size", result);
```
A kibibyte is slightly larger than a kilobyte, so the number is smaller in the result; but other than that, it works in exactly the same way, with the binary prefix being converted to a symbol automatically.

[§](https://docs.rs#which-type-of-prefix-should-i-use)Which type of prefix should I use?

There is no correct answer this question! Common practice is to use
the binary prefixes for numbers of *bytes*, while still using the decimal
prefixes for everything else. Computers work with powers of two, rather than
powers of ten, and by using the binary prefixes, you get a more accurate
representation of the amount of data.

[§](https://docs.rs#prefix-names)Prefix Names

If you need to describe your unit in actual words, rather than just with the
symbol, use one of the `upper`, `caps`, `lower`, or `symbol`, which output the
prefix in a variety of formats. For example:

```
use unit_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    },
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}bytes in size", n, prefix.lower())
    },
};
assert_eq!("The file is 8.5 kilobytes in size", result);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#string-parsing)String Parsing

There is a `FromStr` implementation for `NumberPrefix` that parses
strings containing numbers and trailing prefixes, such as `7.5E`.

Currently, the only supported units are `b` and `B` for bytes, and `m` for
metres. Whitespace is allowed between the number and the rest of the string.

```
use unit_prefix::{NumberPrefix, Prefix};
assert_eq!(
    "7.05E".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
    Ok(NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Exa, 7.05_f64))
);
assert_eq!(
    "7.05".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
    Ok(NumberPrefix::Standalone(7.05_f64))
);
assert_eq!(
    "7.05 GiB".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
    Ok(NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Gibi, 7.05_f64))
);
```
## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Number](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html)- Prefix
- The result of trying to apply a prefix to a floating-point value.
- [Prefix](https://docs.rs/enum.Prefix.html)
- A numeric prefix, either binary or decimal.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Amounts](https://docs.rs/trait.Amounts.html)
- Traits for floating-point values for both the possible multipliers. They need to be Copy, have defined 1000 and 1024s, and implement a bunch of operators.

# unit_prefix/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)#![deny(unsafe_code)]
[2](https://docs.rs#2)#![warn(missing_copy_implementations)]
[3](https://docs.rs#3)#![warn(missing_debug_implementations)]
[4](https://docs.rs#4)#![warn(missing_docs)]

[9](https://docs.rs#9)
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! This is a library for formatting numbers with numeric prefixes, such as
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! turning “3000 metres” into “3 kilometres”, or “8705 bytes” into “8.5 KiB”.
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! # Usage
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//!
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! The function [`NumberPrefix::decimal`](enum.NumberPrefix.html#method.decimal)
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! returns either a pair of the resulting number and its prefix, or a
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! notice that the number was too small to have any prefix applied to it. For
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! example:
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! ```
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! use unit_prefix::NumberPrefix;
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! let amount = 8542_f32;
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!     NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//!         format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!     },
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!     NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//!         format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!     },
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! };
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! assert_eq!("The file is 8.5 kB in size", result);
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! ```
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! The `{:.1}` part of the formatting string tells it to restrict the
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! output to only one decimal place. This value is calculated by repeatedly
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! dividing the number by 1000 until it becomes less than that, which in this
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! case results in 8.542, which gets rounded down. Because only one division
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! had to take place, the function also returns the decimal prefix `Kilo`,
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! which gets converted to its internationally-recognised symbol when
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! formatted as a string.
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! If the value is too small to have any prefixes applied to it — in this case,
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! if it’s under 1000 — then the standalone value will be returned:
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! ```
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! use unit_prefix::NumberPrefix;
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! let amount = 705_f32;
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!     NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!         format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//!     },
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!     NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//!         format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!     },
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! };
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//!
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! assert_eq!("The file is 705 bytes in size", result);
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! ```
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//!
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! In this particular example, the user expects different formatting for
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! both bytes and kilobytes: while prefixed values are given more precision,
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! there’s no point using anything other than whole numbers for just byte
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! amounts. This is why the function pays attention to values without any
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! prefixes — they often need to be special-cased.
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//!
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! ## Binary Prefixes
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//!
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! This library also allows you to use the *binary prefixes*, which use the
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! number 1024 (2<sup>10</sup>) as the multiplier, rather than the more common 1000
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! (10<sup>3</sup>). This uses the
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! [`NumberPrefix::binary`](enum.NumberPrefix.html#method.binary) function.
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! For example:
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! ```
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! use unit_prefix::NumberPrefix;
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! let amount = 8542_f32;
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! let result = match NumberPrefix::binary(amount) {
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//!     NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//!         format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//!     },
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!     NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!         format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//!     },
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! };
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//!
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! assert_eq!("The file is 8.3 KiB in size", result);
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! ```
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! A kibibyte is slightly larger than a kilobyte, so the number is smaller
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! in the result; but other than that, it works in exactly the same way, with
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! the binary prefix being converted to a symbol automatically.
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//!
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//!
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! ## Which type of prefix should I use?
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//!
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! There is no correct answer this question! Common practice is to use
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! the binary prefixes for numbers of *bytes*, while still using the decimal
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! prefixes for everything else. Computers work with powers of two, rather than
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! powers of ten, and by using the binary prefixes, you get a more accurate
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! representation of the amount of data.
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//!
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//!
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! ## Prefix Names
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//!
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! If you need to describe your unit in actual words, rather than just with the
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! symbol, use one of the `upper`, `caps`, `lower`, or `symbol`, which output the
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! prefix in a variety of formats. For example:
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//!
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! ```
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! use unit_prefix::NumberPrefix;
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//!
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! let amount = 8542_f32;
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//!     NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//!         format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//!     },
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//!     NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//!         format!("The file is {:.1} {}bytes in size", n, prefix.lower())
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//!     },
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! };
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//!
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! assert_eq!("The file is 8.5 kilobytes in size", result);
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//! ```
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//!
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! ## String Parsing
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//!
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! There is a `FromStr` implementation for `NumberPrefix` that parses
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//! strings containing numbers and trailing prefixes, such as `7.5E`.
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//!
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! Currently, the only supported units are `b` and `B` for bytes, and `m` for
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! metres. Whitespace is allowed between the number and the rest of the string.
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//!
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! ```
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! use unit_prefix::{NumberPrefix, Prefix};
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//!
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! assert_eq!(
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//!     "7.05E".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//!     Ok(NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Exa, 7.05_f64))
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! );
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//!
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! assert_eq!(
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//!     "7.05".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//!     Ok(NumberPrefix::Standalone(7.05_f64))
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! );
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//!
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! assert_eq!(
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//!     "7.05 GiB".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//!     Ok(NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Gibi, 7.05_f64))
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! );
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! ```
[158](https://docs.rs#158)
[159](https://docs.rs#159)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "std"), no_std)]
[160](https://docs.rs#160)

[178](https://docs.rs#178)    Mega,

[238](https://docs.rs#238)/// The result of trying to apply a prefix to a floating-point value.
[239](https://docs.rs#239)#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, Clone, Debug)]
[240](https://docs.rs#240)pub enum NumberPrefix<F> {
[241](https://docs.rs#241)    /// A **standalone** value is returned when the number is too small to
[242](https://docs.rs#242)    /// have any prefixes applied to it. This is commonly a special case, so
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    /// is handled separately.
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    Standalone(F),
[245](https://docs.rs#245)
[246](https://docs.rs#246)    /// A **prefixed** value *is* large enough for prefixes. This holds the
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    /// prefix, as well as the resulting value.
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    Prefixed(Prefix, F),
[249](https://docs.rs#249)}
[250](https://docs.rs#250)
[251](https://docs.rs#251)impl<F: Amounts> NumberPrefix<F> {
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    /// Formats the given floating-point number using **decimal** prefixes.
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    ///
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    /// This function accepts both `f32` and `f64` values. If you’re trying to
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    /// format an integer, you’ll have to cast it first.
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    ///
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    /// # Examples
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    ///
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    /// ```
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    /// use unit_prefix::{NumberPrefix, Prefix};
[261](https://docs.rs#261)    ///
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    /// assert_eq!(
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    ///     NumberPrefix::decimal(1_000_000_000_f32),
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    ///     NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Giga, 1_f32)
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    /// );
[266](https://docs.rs#266)    /// ```
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    pub fn decimal(amount: F) -> Self {
[268](https://docs.rs#268)        use self::Prefix::*;
[269](https://docs.rs#269)        Self::format_number(
[270](https://docs.rs#270)            amount,
[271](https://docs.rs#271)            Amounts::NUM_1000,
[272](https://docs.rs#272)            [Kilo, Mega, Giga, Tera, Peta, Exa, Zetta, Yotta],
[273](https://docs.rs#273)        )
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    }
[275](https://docs.rs#275)
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    /// Formats the given floating-point number using **binary** prefixes.
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    ///
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    /// This function accepts both `f32` and `f64` values. If you’re trying to
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    /// format an integer, you’ll have to cast it first.
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    ///
[281](https://docs.rs#281)    /// # Examples
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    ///
[283](https://docs.rs#283)    /// ```
[284](https://docs.rs#284)    /// use unit_prefix::{NumberPrefix, Prefix};
[285](https://docs.rs#285)    ///
[286](https://docs.rs#286)    /// assert_eq!(
[287](https://docs.rs#287)    ///     NumberPrefix::binary(1_073_741_824_f64),
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    ///     NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Gibi, 1_f64)
[289](https://docs.rs#289)    /// );
[290](https://docs.rs#290)    /// ```
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    pub fn binary(amount: F) -> Self {
[292](https://docs.rs#292)        use self::Prefix::*;
[293](https://docs.rs#293)        Self::format_number(
[294](https://docs.rs#294)            amount,
[295](https://docs.rs#295)            Amounts::NUM_1024,
[296](https://docs.rs#296)            [Kibi, Mebi, Gibi, Tebi, Pebi, Exbi, Zebi, Yobi],
[297](https://docs.rs#297)        )
[298](https://docs.rs#298)    }
[299](https://docs.rs#299)
[300](https://docs.rs#300)    fn format_number(mut amount: F, kilo: F, prefixes: [Prefix; 8]) -> Self {
[301](https://docs.rs#301)        // For negative numbers, flip it to positive, do the processing, then
[302](https://docs.rs#302)        // flip it back to negative again afterwards.
[303](https://docs.rs#303)        let was_negative = if amount.is_negative() {
[304](https://docs.rs#304)            amount = -amount;
[305](https://docs.rs#305)            true
[306](https://docs.rs#306)        } else {
[307](https://docs.rs#307)            false
[308](https://docs.rs#308)        };
[309](https://docs.rs#309)
[310](https://docs.rs#310)        let mut prefix = 0;
[311](https://docs.rs#311)        while amount >= kilo && prefix < 8 {
[312](https://docs.rs#312)            amount = amount / kilo;
[313](https://docs.rs#313)            prefix += 1;
[314](https://docs.rs#314)        }
[315](https://docs.rs#315)
[316](https://docs.rs#316)        if was_negative {
[317](https://docs.rs#317)            amount = -amount;
[318](https://docs.rs#318)        }
[319](https://docs.rs#319)
[320](https://docs.rs#320)        if prefix == 0 {
[321](https://docs.rs#321)            NumberPrefix::Standalone(amount)
[322](https://docs.rs#322)        } else {
[323](https://docs.rs#323)            NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefixes[prefix - 1], amount)
[324](https://docs.rs#324)        }
[325](https://docs.rs#325)    }
[326](https://docs.rs#326)}
[327](https://docs.rs#327)
[328](https://docs.rs#328)impl fmt::Display for Prefix {
[329](https://docs.rs#329)    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
[330](https://docs.rs#330)        write!(f, "{}", self.symbol())
[331](https://docs.rs#331)    }

[334](https://docs.rs#334)impl Prefix {
[335](https://docs.rs#335)    /// Returns the name in uppercase, such as “KILO”.

[337](https://docs.rs#337)    /// # Examples

[345](https://docs.rs#345)    pub fn upper(self) -> &'static str {
[346](https://docs.rs#346)        use self::Prefix::*;
[347](https://docs.rs#347)        match self {
[348](https://docs.rs#348)            Kilo => "KILO",
[349](https://docs.rs#349)            Mega => "MEGA",
[350](https://docs.rs#350)            Giga => "GIGA",
[351](https://docs.rs#351)            Tera => "TERA",
[352](https://docs.rs#352)            Peta => "PETA",
[353](https://docs.rs#353)            Exa => "EXA",
[354](https://docs.rs#354)            Zetta => "ZETTA",
[355](https://docs.rs#355)            Yotta => "YOTTA",
[356](https://docs.rs#356)            Kibi => "KIBI",
[357](https://docs.rs#357)            Mebi => "MEBI",
[358](https://docs.rs#358)            Gibi => "GIBI",
[359](https://docs.rs#359)            Tebi => "TEBI",
[360](https://docs.rs#360)            Pebi => "PEBI",
[361](https://docs.rs#361)            Exbi => "EXBI",
[362](https://docs.rs#362)            Zebi => "ZEBI",
[363](https://docs.rs#363)            Yobi => "YOBI",
[364](https://docs.rs#364)        }
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    }
[366](https://docs.rs#366)
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    /// Returns the name with the first letter capitalised, such as “Mega”.
[368](https://docs.rs#368)    ///

# NumberPrefix in unit_prefix - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/unit-prefix/0.5.2/unit_prefix/enum.NumberPrefix.html

```
pub enum NumberPrefix<F> {
    Standalone(F),
    Prefixed(
```
[Prefix](https://docs.rs/enum.Prefix.html), F),
}## Expand description

The result of trying to apply a prefix to a floating-point value.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Standalone)

### Standalone(F)

A **standalone** value is returned when the number is too small to
have any prefixes applied to it. This is commonly a special case, so
is handled separately.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Prefixed)

### Prefixed([Prefix](https://docs.rs/enum.Prefix.html), F)

A **prefixed** value *is* large enough for prefixes. This holds the
prefix, as well as the resulting value.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/unit_prefix/lib.rs.html#251-326)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-NumberPrefix%3CF%3E)### impl<F: [Amounts](https://docs.rs/trait.Amounts.html)> [NumberPrefix](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html)<F>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/unit_prefix/lib.rs.html#251-326)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-NumberPrefix%3CF%3E)

### impl<F: [Amounts](https://docs.rs/trait.Amounts.html)> [NumberPrefix](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html)<F>

Formats the given floating-point number using **decimal** prefixes.

This function accepts both `f32` and `f64` values. If you’re trying to
format an integer, you’ll have to cast it first.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use unit_prefix::{NumberPrefix, Prefix};
assert_eq!(
    NumberPrefix::decimal(1_000_000_000_f32),
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Giga, 1_f32)
);
```
```
29fn main() {
30    // part one, decimal prefixes
31    let mut n = 1_f64;
32    for _ in 0..8 {
33        n *= 1000_f64;
34
35        let decimal = format_prefix(NumberPrefix::decimal(n));
36        let binary = format_prefix(NumberPrefix::binary(n));
37        println!("{:26} bytes is {} and {:10}", n, decimal, binary);
38    }
39
40    println!();
41
42    // part two, binary prefixes
43    let mut n = 1_f64;

48        let binary = format_prefix(NumberPrefix::binary(n));

51}

# Prefix in unit_prefix - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/unit-prefix/0.5.2/unit_prefix/enum.Prefix.html

```
pub enum Prefix {
```
## Show 16 variants

    Kilo,
    Mega,
    Giga,
    Tera,
    Peta,
    Exa,
    Zetta,
    Yotta,
    Kibi,
    Mebi,
    Gibi,
    Tebi,
    Pebi,
    Exbi,
    Zebi,
    Yobi,
}## Expand description

A numeric prefix, either binary or decimal.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Kilo)

### Kilo

*kilo*, 103 or 10001.
From the Greek ‘χίλιοι’ (‘chilioi’), meaning ‘thousand’.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Mega)

### Mega

*mega*, 106 or 10002.
From the Ancient Greek ‘μέγας’ (‘megas’), meaning ‘great’.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Giga)

### Giga

*giga*, 109 or 10003.
From the Greek ‘γίγας’ (‘gigas’), meaning ‘giant’.

# unit_prefix - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/unit-prefix/latest/unit_prefix/

## Expand description

This is a library for formatting numbers with numeric prefixes, such as turning “3000 metres” into “3 kilometres”, or “8705 bytes” into “8.5 KiB”.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The function [ NumberPrefix::decimal](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html#method.decimal)
returns either a pair of the resulting number and its prefix, or a
notice that the number was too small to have any prefix applied to it. For
example:

```
use unit_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    },
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
    },
};
assert_eq!("The file is 8.5 kB in size", result);
```
The `{:.1}` part of the formatting string tells it to restrict the
output to only one decimal place. This value is calculated by repeatedly
dividing the number by 1000 until it becomes less than that, which in this
case results in 8.542, which gets rounded down. Because only one division
had to take place, the function also returns the decimal prefix `Kilo`,
which gets converted to its internationally-recognised symbol when
formatted as a string.

If the value is too small to have any prefixes applied to it — in this case, if it’s under 1000 — then the standalone value will be returned:

```
use unit_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 705_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    },
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
    },
};
assert_eq!("The file is 705 bytes in size", result);
```
In this particular example, the user expects different formatting for both bytes and kilobytes: while prefixed values are given more precision, there’s no point using anything other than whole numbers for just byte amounts. This is why the function pays attention to values without any prefixes — they often need to be special-cased.

[§](https://docs.rs#binary-prefixes)Binary Prefixes

This library also allows you to use the *binary prefixes*, which use the
number 1024 (210) as the multiplier, rather than the more common 1000
(103). This uses the
[ NumberPrefix::binary](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html#method.binary) function.
For example:

```
use unit_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::binary(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    },
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
    },
};
assert_eq!("The file is 8.3 KiB in size", result);
```
A kibibyte is slightly larger than a kilobyte, so the number is smaller in the result; but other than that, it works in exactly the same way, with the binary prefix being converted to a symbol automatically.

[§](https://docs.rs#which-type-of-prefix-should-i-use)Which type of prefix should I use?

There is no correct answer this question! Common practice is to use
the binary prefixes for numbers of *bytes*, while still using the decimal
prefixes for everything else. Computers work with powers of two, rather than
powers of ten, and by using the binary prefixes, you get a more accurate
representation of the amount of data.

[§](https://docs.rs#prefix-names)Prefix Names

If you need to describe your unit in actual words, rather than just with the
symbol, use one of the `upper`, `caps`, `lower`, or `symbol`, which output the
prefix in a variety of formats. For example:

```
use unit_prefix::NumberPrefix;
let amount = 8542_f32;
let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
    NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
        format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
    },
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
        format!("The file is {:.1} {}bytes in size", n, prefix.lower())
    },
};
assert_eq!("The file is 8.5 kilobytes in size", result);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#string-parsing)String Parsing

There is a `FromStr` implementation for `NumberPrefix` that parses
strings containing numbers and trailing prefixes, such as `7.5E`.

Currently, the only supported units are `b` and `B` for bytes, and `m` for
metres. Whitespace is allowed between the number and the rest of the string.

```
use unit_prefix::{NumberPrefix, Prefix};
assert_eq!(
    "7.05E".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
    Ok(NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Exa, 7.05_f64))
);
assert_eq!(
    "7.05".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
    Ok(NumberPrefix::Standalone(7.05_f64))
);
assert_eq!(
    "7.05 GiB".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
    Ok(NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Gibi, 7.05_f64))
);
```
## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Number](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html)- Prefix
- The result of trying to apply a prefix to a floating-point value.
- [Prefix](https://docs.rs/enum.Prefix.html)
- A numeric prefix, either binary or decimal.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Amounts](https://docs.rs/trait.Amounts.html)
- Traits for floating-point values for both the possible multipliers. They need to be Copy, have defined 1000 and 1024s, and implement a bunch of operators.

[§](https://docs.rs#string-parsing)String Parsing

There is a `FromStr` implementation for `NumberPrefix` that parses
strings containing numbers and trailing prefixes, such as `7.5E`.

Currently, the only supported units are `b` and `B` for bytes, and `m` for
metres. Whitespace is allowed between the number and the rest of the string.

```
use unit_prefix::{NumberPrefix, Prefix};
assert_eq!(
    "7.05E".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
    Ok(NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Exa, 7.05_f64))
);
assert_eq!(
    "7.05".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
    Ok(NumberPrefix::Standalone(7.05_f64))
);
assert_eq!(
    "7.05 GiB".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
    Ok(NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Gibi, 7.05_f64))
);
```
## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Number](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html)- Prefix
- The result of trying to apply a prefix to a floating-point value.
- [Prefix](https://docs.rs/enum.Prefix.html)
- A numeric prefix, either binary or decimal.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Amounts](https://docs.rs/trait.Amounts.html)
- Traits for floating-point values for both the possible multipliers. They need to be Copy, have defined 1000 and 1024s, and implement a bunch of operators.

# unit_prefix/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)#![deny(unsafe_code)]
[2](https://docs.rs#2)#![warn(missing_copy_implementations)]
[3](https://docs.rs#3)#![warn(missing_debug_implementations)]
[4](https://docs.rs#4)#![warn(missing_docs)]
[5](https://docs.rs#5)#![warn(nonstandard_style)]
[6](https://docs.rs#6)#![warn(trivial_numeric_casts)]
[7](https://docs.rs#7)#![warn(unreachable_pub)]
[8](https://docs.rs#8)#![warn(unused)]
[9](https://docs.rs#9)
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! This is a library for formatting numbers with numeric prefixes, such as
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! turning “3000 metres” into “3 kilometres”, or “8705 bytes” into “8.5 KiB”.
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! # Usage
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//!
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! The function [`NumberPrefix::decimal`](enum.NumberPrefix.html#method.decimal)
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! returns either a pair of the resulting number and its prefix, or a
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! notice that the number was too small to have any prefix applied to it. For
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! example:
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! ```
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! use unit_prefix::NumberPrefix;
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! let amount = 8542_f32;
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!     NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//!         format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!     },
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!     NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//!         format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!     },
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! };
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! assert_eq!("The file is 8.5 kB in size", result);
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! ```
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! The `{:.1}` part of the formatting string tells it to restrict the
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! output to only one decimal place. This value is calculated by repeatedly
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! dividing the number by 1000 until it becomes less than that, which in this
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! case results in 8.542, which gets rounded down. Because only one division
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! had to take place, the function also returns the decimal prefix `Kilo`,
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! which gets converted to its internationally-recognised symbol when
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! formatted as a string.
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! If the value is too small to have any prefixes applied to it — in this case,
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! if it’s under 1000 — then the standalone value will be returned:
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! ```
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! use unit_prefix::NumberPrefix;
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! let amount = 705_f32;
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!     NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!         format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//!     },
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!     NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//!         format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!     },
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! };
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//!
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! assert_eq!("The file is 705 bytes in size", result);
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! ```
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//!
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! In this particular example, the user expects different formatting for
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! both bytes and kilobytes: while prefixed values are given more precision,
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! there’s no point using anything other than whole numbers for just byte
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! amounts. This is why the function pays attention to values without any
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! prefixes — they often need to be special-cased.
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//!
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! ## Binary Prefixes
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//!
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! This library also allows you to use the *binary prefixes*, which use the
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! number 1024 (2<sup>10</sup>) as the multiplier, rather than the more common 1000
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! (10<sup>3</sup>). This uses the
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! [`NumberPrefix::binary`](enum.NumberPrefix.html#method.binary) function.
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! For example:
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! ```
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! use unit_prefix::NumberPrefix;
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! let amount = 8542_f32;
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! let result = match NumberPrefix::binary(amount) {
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//!     NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//!         format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//!     },
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!     NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!         format!("The file is {:.1} {}B in size", n, prefix)
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//!     },
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! };
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//!
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! assert_eq!("The file is 8.3 KiB in size", result);
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! ```
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! A kibibyte is slightly larger than a kilobyte, so the number is smaller
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! in the result; but other than that, it works in exactly the same way, with
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! the binary prefix being converted to a symbol automatically.
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//!
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//!
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! ## Which type of prefix should I use?
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//!
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! There is no correct answer this question! Common practice is to use
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! the binary prefixes for numbers of *bytes*, while still using the decimal
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! prefixes for everything else. Computers work with powers of two, rather than
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! powers of ten, and by using the binary prefixes, you get a more accurate
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! representation of the amount of data.
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//!
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//!
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! ## Prefix Names
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//!
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! If you need to describe your unit in actual words, rather than just with the
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! symbol, use one of the `upper`, `caps`, `lower`, or `symbol`, which output the
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! prefix in a variety of formats. For example:
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//!
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! ```
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! use unit_prefix::NumberPrefix;
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//!
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! let amount = 8542_f32;
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! let result = match NumberPrefix::decimal(amount) {
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//!     NumberPrefix::Standalone(bytes) => {
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//!         format!("The file is {} bytes in size", bytes)
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//!     },
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//!     NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefix, n) => {
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//!         format!("The file is {:.1} {}bytes in size", n, prefix.lower())
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//!     },
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! };
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//!
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! assert_eq!("The file is 8.5 kilobytes in size", result);
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//! ```
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//!
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! ## String Parsing
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//!
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! There is a `FromStr` implementation for `NumberPrefix` that parses
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//! strings containing numbers and trailing prefixes, such as `7.5E`.
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//!
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! Currently, the only supported units are `b` and `B` for bytes, and `m` for
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! metres. Whitespace is allowed between the number and the rest of the string.
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//!
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! ```
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! use unit_prefix::{NumberPrefix, Prefix};
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//!
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! assert_eq!(
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//!     "7.05E".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//!     Ok(NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Exa, 7.05_f64))
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! );
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//!
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! assert_eq!(
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//!     "7.05".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//!     Ok(NumberPrefix::Standalone(7.05_f64))
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! );
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//!
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! assert_eq!(
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//!     "7.05 GiB".parse::<NumberPrefix<_>>(),
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//!     Ok(NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Gibi, 7.05_f64))
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! );
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! ```
[158](https://docs.rs#158)
[159](https://docs.rs#159)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "std"), no_std)]

[238](https://docs.rs#238)/// The result of trying to apply a prefix to a floating-point value.
[239](https://docs.rs#239)#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, Clone, Debug)]
[240](https://docs.rs#240)pub enum NumberPrefix<F> {
[241](https://docs.rs#241)    /// A **standalone** value is returned when the number is too small to
[242](https://docs.rs#242)    /// have any prefixes applied to it. This is commonly a special case, so
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    /// is handled separately.
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    Standalone(F),
[245](https://docs.rs#245)
[246](https://docs.rs#246)    /// A **prefixed** value *is* large enough for prefixes. This holds the
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    /// prefix, as well as the resulting value.
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    Prefixed(Prefix, F),
[249](https://docs.rs#249)}
[250](https://docs.rs#250)
[251](https://docs.rs#251)impl<F: Amounts> NumberPrefix<F> {
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    /// Formats the given floating-point number using **decimal** prefixes.
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    ///
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    /// This function accepts both `f32` and `f64` values. If you’re trying to
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    /// format an integer, you’ll have to cast it first.
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    ///
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    /// # Examples
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    ///
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    /// ```
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    /// use unit_prefix::{NumberPrefix, Prefix};
[261](https://docs.rs#261)    ///
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    /// assert_eq!(
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    ///     NumberPrefix::decimal(1_000_000_000_f32),
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    ///     NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Giga, 1_f32)
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    /// );
[266](https://docs.rs#266)    /// ```
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    pub fn decimal(amount: F) -> Self {
[268](https://docs.rs#268)        use self::Prefix::*;
[269](https://docs.rs#269)        Self::format_number(
[270](https://docs.rs#270)            amount,
[271](https://docs.rs#271)            Amounts::NUM_1000,
[272](https://docs.rs#272)            [Kilo, Mega, Giga, Tera, Peta, Exa, Zetta, Yotta],
[273](https://docs.rs#273)        )
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    }
[275](https://docs.rs#275)
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    /// Formats the given floating-point number using **binary** prefixes.
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    ///
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    /// This function accepts both `f32` and `f64` values. If you’re trying to
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    /// format an integer, you’ll have to cast it first.
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    ///
[281](https://docs.rs#281)    /// # Examples
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    ///
[283](https://docs.rs#283)    /// ```
[284](https://docs.rs#284)    /// use unit_prefix::{NumberPrefix, Prefix};
[285](https://docs.rs#285)    ///
[286](https://docs.rs#286)    /// assert_eq!(
[287](https://docs.rs#287)    ///     NumberPrefix::binary(1_073_741_824_f64),
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    ///     NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Gibi, 1_f64)
[289](https://docs.rs#289)    /// );
[290](https://docs.rs#290)    /// ```
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    pub fn binary(amount: F) -> Self {
[292](https://docs.rs#292)        use self::Prefix::*;
[293](https://docs.rs#293)        Self::format_number(
[294](https://docs.rs#294)            amount,
[295](https://docs.rs#295)            Amounts::NUM_1024,
[296](https://docs.rs#296)            [Kibi, Mebi, Gibi, Tebi, Pebi, Exbi, Zebi, Yobi],
[297](https://docs.rs#297)        )
[298](https://docs.rs#298)    }
[299](https://docs.rs#299)
[300](https://docs.rs#300)    fn format_number(mut amount: F, kilo: F, prefixes: [Prefix; 8]) -> Self {
[301](https://docs.rs#301)        // For negative numbers, flip it to positive, do the processing, then
[302](https://docs.rs#302)        // flip it back to negative again afterwards.
[303](https://docs.rs#303)        let was_negative = if amount.is_negative() {
[304](https://docs.rs#304)            amount = -amount;
[305](https://docs.rs#305)            true
[306](https://docs.rs#306)        } else {
[307](https://docs.rs#307)            false
[308](https://docs.rs#308)        };
[309](https://docs.rs#309)
[310](https://docs.rs#310)        let mut prefix = 0;
[311](https://docs.rs#311)        while amount >= kilo && prefix < 8 {
[312](https://docs.rs#312)            amount = amount / kilo;
[313](https://docs.rs#313)            prefix += 1;
[314](https://docs.rs#314)        }
[315](https://docs.rs#315)
[316](https://docs.rs#316)        if was_negative {
[317](https://docs.rs#317)            amount = -amount;
[318](https://docs.rs#318)        }
[319](https://docs.rs#319)
[320](https://docs.rs#320)        if prefix == 0 {
[321](https://docs.rs#321)            NumberPrefix::Standalone(amount)
[322](https://docs.rs#322)        } else {
[323](https://docs.rs#323)            NumberPrefix::Prefixed(prefixes[prefix - 1], amount)
[324](https://docs.rs#324)        }
[325](https://docs.rs#325)    }
[326](https://docs.rs#326)}
[327](https://docs.rs#327)
[328](https://docs.rs#328)impl fmt::Display for Prefix {
[329](https://docs.rs#329)    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
[330](https://docs.rs#330)        write!(f, "{}", self.symbol())
[331](https://docs.rs#331)    }
[332](https://docs.rs#332)}
[333](https://docs.rs#333)
[334](https://docs.rs#334)impl Prefix {
[335](https://docs.rs#335)    /// Returns the name in uppercase, such as “KILO”.
[336](https://docs.rs#336)    ///
[337](https://docs.rs#337)    /// # Examples
[338](https://docs.rs#338)    ///
[339](https://docs.rs#339)    /// ```
[340](https://docs.rs#340)    /// use unit_prefix::Prefix;
[341](https://docs.rs#341)    ///
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    /// assert_eq!("GIGA", Prefix::Giga.upper());
[343](https://docs.rs#343)    /// assert_eq!("GIBI", Prefix::Gibi.upper());
[344](https://docs.rs#344)    /// ```
[345](https://docs.rs#345)    pub fn upper(self) -> &'static str {
[346](https://docs.rs#346)        use self::Prefix::*;
[347](https://docs.rs#347)        match self {

# NumberPrefix in unit_prefix - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/unit-prefix/latest/target-redirect/unit_prefix/enum.NumberPrefix.html

```
pub enum NumberPrefix<F> {
    Standalone(F),
    Prefixed(
```
[Prefix](https://docs.rs/enum.Prefix.html), F),
}## Expand description

The result of trying to apply a prefix to a floating-point value.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Standalone)

### Standalone(F)

A **standalone** value is returned when the number is too small to
have any prefixes applied to it. This is commonly a special case, so
is handled separately.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Prefixed)

### Prefixed([Prefix](https://docs.rs/enum.Prefix.html), F)

A **prefixed** value *is* large enough for prefixes. This holds the
prefix, as well as the resulting value.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/unit_prefix/lib.rs.html#251-326)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-NumberPrefix%3CF%3E)### impl<F: [Amounts](https://docs.rs/trait.Amounts.html)> [NumberPrefix](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html)<F>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/unit_prefix/lib.rs.html#251-326)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-NumberPrefix%3CF%3E)

### impl<F: [Amounts](https://docs.rs/trait.Amounts.html)> [NumberPrefix](https://docs.rs/enum.NumberPrefix.html)<F>

Formats the given floating-point number using **decimal** prefixes.

This function accepts both `f32` and `f64` values. If you’re trying to
format an integer, you’ll have to cast it first.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use unit_prefix::{NumberPrefix, Prefix};
assert_eq!(
    NumberPrefix::decimal(1_000_000_000_f32),
    NumberPrefix::Prefixed(Prefix::Giga, 1_f32)
);
```
```
29fn main() {
30    // part one, decimal prefixes
31    let mut n = 1_f64;
32    for _ in 0..8 {
33        n *= 1000_f64;
34
35        let decimal = format_prefix(NumberPrefix::decimal(n));
36        let binary = format_prefix(NumberPrefix::binary(n));
37        println!("{:26} bytes is {} and {:10}", n, decimal, binary);
38    }
39
40    println!();
41
42    // part two, binary prefixes
43    let mut n = 1_f64;
44    for _ in 0..8 {
45        n *= 1024_f64;
46
47        let decimal = format_prefix(NumberPrefix::decimal(n));
48        let binary = format_prefix(NumberPrefix::binary(n));
49        println!("{:26} bytes is {} and {:10}", n, binary, decimal);
50    }
51}
```
Formats the given floating-point number using **binary** prefixes.

This function accepts both `f32` and `f64` values. If you’re trying to
format an integer, you’ll have to cast it first.

# clap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/clap

## Expand description

Command Line Argument Parser for Rust

Quick Links:

- Derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)
- Builder [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_tutorial/index.html)and[reference](https://docs.rs/struct.Command.html)
- [Cookbook](https://docs.rs/_cookbook/index.html)
- [CLI Concepts](https://docs.rs/_concepts/index.html)
- [FAQ](https://docs.rs/_faq/index.html)
- [Discussions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/discussions)
- [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/blob/v4.6.1/CHANGELOG.md)(includes major version migration guides)

[§](https://docs.rs#aspirations)Aspirations

- Out of the box, users get a polished CLI experience
- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output, [shell completions](https://github.com/clap-rs/clap/tree/master/clap_complete), etc

- Including common argument behavior, help generation, suggested fixes for users, colored output,
- Flexible enough to port your existing CLI interface
- However, we won’t necessarily streamline support for each use case

- Reasonable parse performance
- Resilient maintainership, including
- Willing to break compatibility rather than batching up breaking changes in large releases
- Leverage feature flags to keep to one active branch
- Being under [WG-CLI](https://github.com/rust-cli/team/)to increase the bus factor

- We follow semver and will wait about 6-9 months between major breaking changes
- We will support the last two minor Rust releases (MSRV, currently 1.74)

While these aspirations can be at odds with fast build times and low binary
size, we will still strive to keep these reasonable for the flexibility you
get.  Check out the
[argparse-benchmarks](https://github.com/rust-cli/argparse-benchmarks-rs) for
CLI parsers optimized for other use cases.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Run

`$ cargo add clap --features derive`*(See also  feature flag reference)*

Then define your CLI in `main.rs`:

```
use clap::Parser;
/// Simple program to greet a person
#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(version, about, long_about = None)]
struct Args {
    /// Name of the person to greet
    #[arg(short, long)]
    name: String,
    /// Number of times to greet
    #[arg(short, long, default_value_t = 1)]
    count: u8,
}
fn main() {
    let args = Args::parse();
    for _ in 0..args.count {
        println!("Hello {}!", args.name);
    }
}
```
And try it out:

```
$ demo --help
A simple to use, efficient, and full-featured Command Line Argument Parser
Usage: demo[EXE] [OPTIONS] --name <NAME>
Options:
  -n, --name <NAME>    Name of the person to greet
  -c, --count <COUNT>  Number of times to greet [default: 1]
  -h, --help           Print help
  -V, --version        Print version
$ demo --name Me
Hello Me!
```
*(version number and  .exe extension on windows replaced by placeholders)*

See also the derive [tutorial](https://docs.rs/_derive/_tutorial/index.html) and [reference](https://docs.rs/_derive/index.html)

CLI Helpers
